chapter.title: What it owns: assets, fast and slow

cards.body: Walk through the house. In the kitchen drawer there is some cash, in the fridge there is food you will eat this week, and the neighbour still owes you 50 for the old lawnmower. Those are *fast*: they are cash, or will be soon. The house, the boiler and the car on the drive are *slow*: you could sell them, but not this month and not without fuss. **A balance sheet lists what a company owns from fastest to slowest.**
cards.simpler: Think about your own home. There is some cash in a drawer, food in the fridge you will eat this week, and a neighbour who owes you 50 for an old lawnmower. These are fast. They are cash now or will be soon. The house, the boiler and the car are slow. You could sell them, but not this month and not easily. **A balance sheet lists what a company owns from fastest to slowest.**

cards.prompt: Mo runs a bakery and needs 500 by Friday. Which of these turns into cash soonest?

options.text: The 40 loaves cooling on the shelf

whyNot.a: That's a slow asset, not a fast one: an oven can be sold, but not by Friday and not for what she paid.
whyNot.c: That's the slowest kind, not a fast one: a lease is a right to use the shop for years, not something she can cash in this week.

cards.reteach: Ask one question of each thing: how soon could this be money in the till? Bread sells today. Ovens and leases sit still. The sheet sorts by that question, nothing fancier.

cards.title: The line at 12 months
cards.body:
Accountants draw one line, at 12 months. Anything the company expects to turn into cash within a year sits above it and is called a *current asset*, which just means fast.

Three things live there in nearly every company. Cash, which needs no explaining. *Receivables*, invoices the company has sent to customers who have not paid yet. And *inventory*, the stock sitting on shelves or in a warehouse, waiting to be sold.

**They appear in that order, most cash-like first.** A customer's invoice is usually closer to money than a box of unsold stock.
cards.simpler:
Accountants draw one line at 12 months. Anything the company expects to turn into cash within a year goes above the line. These are called current assets, which means fast.

Three things almost always sit there. Cash. Receivables, which are bills sent to customers who have not paid yet. And inventory, which is stock on shelves waiting to be sold.

**They appear in that order, most cash-like first.** An unpaid bill is usually closer to money than unsold stock.

cards.title: Rosa's bike shop, 31 December
cards.body: Rosa's balance sheet shows cash 12,000, customer invoices 5,000, bikes in stock 48,000, the shop building 200,000 and workshop tools 15,000. Total assets: 280,000. Rosa feels like a woman with 280,000. But **only 65,000 is fast**, and 48,000 of that is bicycles in a town where it is snowing. The money she can actually spend tomorrow is 12,000. The building is most of her wealth and the least useful thing for paying January's electricity bill.
cards.simpler: Rosa's bike shop closes its books on 31 December. She has cash of 12,000, unpaid customer bills of 5,000, bikes in stock worth 48,000, a shop building worth 200,000 and tools worth 15,000. Total: 280,000. Rosa feels rich. But **only 65,000 is fast**, and 48,000 of that is bicycles in a snowy town. The money she can spend tomorrow is 12,000. The building is most of her wealth, yet it cannot pay January's electricity bill.

cards.prompt: A courier firm's sheet lists: two vans bought last year, 3,000 of invoices customers have not paid yet, and a 20-year lease on its depot. Which line is a current asset?

whyNot.a: That's a long-term asset, not a current one: vans are used for years, not turned into cash within 12 months.
whyNot.c: That's a long-term asset, not a current one: a 20-year lease is a right to stay, and it stays slow for 20 years.

cards.reteach: Current means cash within 12 months. Invoices get paid in weeks, so they count. Vans and leases are kept and used, so they sit below the line as slow.

cards.title: Below the line
cards.body:
Under the 12-month line sit the *non-current assets*, the slow ones: land, buildings, machines, vehicles. The sheet shows them at what they cost minus *depreciation*, the accountant's steady guess at wear and tear. That is not what they would sell for today.

One odd line hides here: *goodwill*, or *intangibles*. When a company buys another company and pays more than its stuff is worth, the extra is parked here. It stands for a brand, a customer list, a reputation. It cannot be sold on its own.

**Your job is to find the two or three biggest lines** and ask of each: how soon could this be cash?
cards.simpler:
Below the 12-month line sit the slow ones, called non-current assets: buildings, machines, vehicles. They appear at cost minus depreciation, a steady guess at wear and tear, not today's selling price.

One odd line hides here: goodwill, or intangibles. If a company buys another for more than its stuff is worth, the extra sits here. It stands for a brand or reputation and cannot be sold alone.

**Find the two or three biggest lines** and ask when each could be cash.

cards.body: Priya reads total assets of 9 million and relaxes. Then she looks closer: 7 million of it is one line, goodwill from buying a rival 3 years ago. Nothing in that 7 million can be sold, and the company has 400,000 in cash. **Spot it by finding the biggest line first**, then asking when it could become money. If the honest answer is never on its own, the total is mostly a memory of a purchase.
cards.simpler: Priya sees total assets of 9 million and relaxes. Then she looks closer. 7 million of it is one line: goodwill from buying a rival 3 years ago. None of that 7 million can be sold, and the company has only 400,000 in cash. **Spot it by finding the biggest line first**, then ask when it could become money. If the honest answer is never on its own, the total is mostly a memory of a purchase.

cards.prompt: Why does a balance sheet split what a company owns into two groups?

options.text: To show which things cost the most
To show which things could become cash within 12 months and which cannot
To show which things were bought this year

whyNot.a: That's size, not speed: a building can be the biggest line and still the slowest to turn into cash.
whyNot.c: That's the purchase date, not the cash date: a van bought last week is still a slow asset because it will be used for years.

cards.reteach: The split is about time to cash. Above the line: cash, unpaid customer invoices and stock, all expected to be money within a year. Below the line: buildings, machines and bought brands, which the company keeps and uses.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Everything a company owns is listed fastest to slowest: cash, unpaid customer invoices and stock above the 12-month line, buildings, machines and bought-in brands below it. **Find the biggest two or three lines and ask how soon each could be cash.**
cards.simpler: Everything a company owns is listed from fastest to slowest. Above the 12-month line sit cash, unpaid customer bills and stock. Below it sit buildings, machines and bought-in brands. **Find the biggest two or three lines and ask how soon each could be cash.**

cards.body: Search online for any listed company's annual report and find the balance sheet. Write down total current assets, total assets and the single biggest line. Say out loud whether that biggest line is fast or slow.
cards.simpler: Search online for the annual report of any listed company, meaning one whose shares you can buy on a stock exchange. Find the balance sheet inside it. Write down three numbers: total current assets, total assets and the single biggest line. Then say out loud whether that biggest line is fast or slow.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now sort every asset line into fast or slow and name the biggest things a company owns.
